newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: OPINION - Philippines peso - Goldman Sachs.
newsitem.headline: OPINION - Philippines peso - Goldman Sachs.
newsitem.byline: Goldman Sachs Asia Economic Research Group

text.p: Does the Philippines have a peso problem? The nominal peso dollar exchange rate has been virtualy pegged at 26.2 pesos per $1.0 for the last 10 months.
Strong capital inflows have boosted international reserves by $3.9 billion as Bangko Sentral (central bank) has attempted to stem nominal appreciation.

Meanwhile, domestic CPI inflation has been 9.9 percent, much more than its trading partners, especially the U.S., which has seen CPI inflation in the last 10 months of only 2.7 percent. As a result, the real exchange rate with the U.S. has moved seven percent.

Concerns about the peso bring up the obvious question of whether this movement in the REER (real effective exchange rate) over the last year is consistent with movement in the country's long-run equilibrium exchange rate.

Although initial work showed large overvaluation, correcting for 1992 changes in the convertibility of the peso and significance of worker's remittances in the financing trade shows the current nominal exchange rate against the dollar of 26.2 pesos is 1.6 percent overvalued relative to long-run equilibrium GSDEEMER (Goldman Sachs dynamic equilibrium emerging market exchange rate) estimates.
This modest overvaluation may be larger due to productivity trends, though data to support this direcly are unavailable.
Consistent with this long-run view, we still expect modest depreciation of the peso to 26.4 per $1.0 by year-end, and 27.3 per $1.0 on a 12-month horizon.
Given current interest differentials of about 550 bp in three months against expected depreciation of 310 bp, being long on the peso is mildly attractive.
BACKGROUND

The Philippines has received significant investor attention over the last year as it has pulled out of the economic muddle that characterized most of the 1980s and early 1990s. The elimination of most capital controls, the reorganization of the central bank, lower import tariff, more open direct investment laws, and a significant improvement in fiscal policy have all played a part in generating higher GDP growth.

Over the last 11 months, the reforms have also generated strong capital inflows which have boosted international reserves by $3.9 billion as Bangko Sentral has attempted to stem nominal appreciation of the peso.

While the nominal dollar peso exchange rate has been virtually pegged at 26.2 pesos for the last ten months, domestic CPI inflation has been 9.9 percent, much more than its trading partners, especially the United States, which has seen CPI inflation rise only 2.7 percent in that time.
We estimate the Philippines real effective exchange rate (REER) relative to the United States has appreciated 7 percent since the beginning of last November.
The change in the REER has generated discussion within the Philippine government about whether there is a need to depreciate the nominal exchange rate.
Total export growth has slipped to only 10.8 percent in August, well down from the 30 percent posted last year, leading to pressure from exporters for depreciation.
Concerns about the peso bring up the obvious question of whether movement in the REER over the last year is consistent with the movement in the country's long-run equilibrium exchage rate.
In the case of the Philippines, our preliminary GSDEEMER analysis on quarterly data from 1981 showed signicant 22.5 percent overvaluation of the peso.
This striking result, however, is at odds with our sense of development in the Philippine equilibrium real exchange rate.

Some of the recent appreciation of the REER is due to changes in the long-run equilibrium exchange rate. The sheer pace of capital inflows that marked 1994 (prior to Mexico's devaluation) and late 1995-1996 parallels the experience of many other emerging market economies which have instituted credible, thorough-going reforms (e.g, Chile in 1989-1990, Peru in 1994).
The capital inflows associated with the return of flight capital, and investment in new opportunities opened up by the reforms clearly pressure currencies higher.

In the case of the Philippines, with export growth still outperforming its neighboring countries, despite its near 40 percent concentration in electronics, it is simply not the case that the currency is 22.5 percent overvalued.
AUGMENTING GSDEEMER FOR THE PHILIPPINES

There are several reasons to believe that in the case of the Philippines, our preliminary analysis is misleading. As a result, we have refined the analysis along the lines presented below. The first sign of a problem with our preliminary analysis was the explanatory power of our GSDEEMER regression.
For a sample period of first quarter 1981 to first-quarter 1996, only about 51 percent of the variance in the real exchange rate was captured by the regression.
This is well below levels for other countries in Asia or Latin America. Why would the model fit so poorly ?

The key is both the turmoil experienced in the Philippines in the 1980s and the relatively short time period since reforms were undertaken in the early 1990s. Perhaps the two most important events were the almost complete convertibility of the peso beginning in third-quarter 1992, and the increased long-term capital flows that have followed the investment liberalization.
Another element of the problem is the importance of overseas worker remittances in financing the current account.
Such worker remittances have grown to annualized levels in 1996 of $6.0 billion from $1.6 billion in 1991, covering almost half of the trade imbalance.
These flows are not strictly capital flows used in balance of payments accounting, they are funds available to meet short falls in the real appreciation of the currency.
The new data dramatically improves the fit of the equation. Rather than explaning only 45 percent of the movement in the REER, the new equation explains over 80 percent.

The convertibility dummy is highly significant, and associated with a more appreciated real exchange rate. So too are worker remittances. Revisions to the long-term capital flow series also boosts its significance in explaning the real exchange rate. Because of the relatively short time period covering the structural changes in the economy, we checked the stability of the estimated coefficients and found them remarkably robust throughout the sample period.

On the basis of the augmented regression work, we estimate the current nominal peso dollar exchange rate of 26.2 pesos per $1.0 is only 1.6 percent overvalued versus what is consistent with long-run equilibrium.
Given the confidence intervals around our point estimates, our GSDEEMER analysis tells us the peso is very close to fair value.
There is reason to believe that even the small degree of undervaluation in our GSDEEMER may be exaggerated.

Like most other countries in Asia, productivity data is largely unavailable. Manufacturing survey data provides some information on employment and output, allowing crude calculations of manufacturing productivity,

However, the authorities have discontinued collection of the employment data because of poor coverage and definitional problems. Furthermore, the productivity data covers only manufacturing but has too short a time span to be include in our regression analysis.

A look at recent export performance, however, hints that diferrential productivity growth may explain some of the appreciation in the REER. Total export growth for the year to August was 19.3 percent.
This figure, however, masks a sharp divergence across sectors. Electronics, components, and peripherals have grown 28 percent.

Traditional labor-intensive exports, such as garments or footwear, have shown sharp contractions. If productivity improvements were bidding up the general level of wages, one would expect to see just such a pattern in the export sector.
If higher wages, driven by higher productivity, were also spilling over into non-traded goods, one would expect higher non-traded goods prices, which is the case.
OUR PESO FORECAST
Given our more complete GSDEEMER estimate, our nominal exchange rate forecast shows only modest depreciation over the course of the next year.

The widening trade imbalance and a moderate slowdown should create pressure for the peso to weaken. The central bank is clearly pushing for a slightly weaker peso, through weaker intervention and interest rates.
With domestic inflation also coming off, there is scope to mudge interest rates lower, another factor behind our view of modest weakening.
Furthermore, any sharp movement toward depreciation is likely to be met with a temporary boost in interest rates, as in early September and in the aftermath of the Mexican devaluation.
The case for at most modest weakening is backed up by our short-term market pressure indicators that point toward modest appreciation.

With fiscal reform likely to ensure continued improvements in the fiscal balance, investor confidence in the Philippines' ability to maintain macro balance should ensure that any weakening in the peso will be mild at best.
(The opinions expressed in this article represent those of the author only. They should not be seen to represent the view of Reuters)
